newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais begin voting after dirty, violent campaign.
newsitem.headline: Thais begin voting after dirty, violent campaign.

text.p: Thais walked, drove and even rowed through flooded waters on Sunday to cast their ballots in a general election following one of the most violent and dirty campaigns seen in decades.

Polling stations opened at 8 a.m. (0100 GMT), and more than 38 million Thais were eligible to cast ballots in the election which is expected to be a close race between the Democrat Party led by former premier Chuan Leekpai and the New Aspiration Party (NAP) of Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.
Opinion polls are divided and the two front-running parties, which are forecast to win about 125 seats each, expect a wafer-thin victory margin.
Turnout was expected to be heavy as people lined up to vote under clear skies in most parts of Thailand.

Former army chief Chavalit, whose party has been a partner in the last two coalition governments, was surrounded by crowds of well-wishers as he went to cast his ballot at a Buddhist temple in Nakhon Panom in northeastern Thailand.
"I call on as many people as possible to come out and exercise their right to vote," Chavalit said after casting his ballot.

Chuan, who was Thailand's longest-serving, democratically elected prime minister before being forced to dissolve parliament after a land scandal in May 1995, was also expected to vote early in southern Thailand's Trang province.

A total of 2,310 candidates from 13 parties are vying for 393 seats in this election, the country's second in 16 months, after Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa dissolved parliament in September and set snap polls.

The party winning the most seats has the right to form a new government. But no one party has ever won enough seats to hold a parliamentary majority, so the government is traditionally a coalition of several parties.

In the capital of Bangkok, where only about 10 percent of the seats are up for grabs, normally traffic-clogged streets were virtually empty as many residents had travelled to their home provinces to vote.
Residents in Pathum Thani, 46 km (28 miles) northwest of Bangkok, rowed through flooded streets to get to the polling booths.
Sunday's vote brings an end to what many are calling the dirtiest and most violent campaign in decades.

Billions of baht have been used by politicians in this election, and at least eight political workers have been shot dead by gunmen. Dozens of others have also been attacked while campaigning, police said.
One voter in Nonthaburi, on the outskirts of Bangkok, said she hoped this was the last time "old-style" money politicking would be seen.
"This is expected to be the last old-style election. We hope the next election will be cleaner after political reform," said Surat Manmek, as she waited to vote.
